newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW-Ferrari mulls technology sale and sharing.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Ferrari mulls technology sale and sharing.

text.p: Italian luxury sports car maker Ferrari is mulling the sale of technology from its Formula One racing cars and sharing investment for research and development, chairman Luca Cordero di Montezemolo said on Monday.
"I'm thinking of the possibility ...to sell to somebody our technology, Formula One maybe," Montezemolo told Reuters in an interview.
"The second possibility is to share investments for very specific research programmes," which could be new electronic technology for a gear box or engine parts, he said.
Ferrari could act on these ideas in a year's time, he said.

Montezemolo, who was in Singapore to launch the firm's 550 Maranello sports coupe, said Ferrari spends heavily on research and development, 20 percent of turnover being spent on road cars and more for its Formula One racing cars.
He said Ferrari came up with new technology for Formula One cars every 12 months and the previous technology could be sold.

The sharing of investment for specific research and development could see Ferrari having exclusive rights to the resulting technology for one to two years, after which its partner could either sell the technology or utilise it.
Ferrari would not discount finding partners for these ventures in Asia, said Montezemolo.
He said Ferrari had no intention of producing outside of its site at Maranello in Italy and would not increase its production of 3,500 cars a year.
It wants to maintain a split of 40 percent to 45 percent of its sales from Europe, 20 percent from the United States, 20 percent from Asia and the remainder from the rest of the world.
For its latest 550 model, it aimed to sell 900 cars by 1997.
The company expects total turnover to reach US$500 million in 1996, which would be growth of slightly over 10 percent from 1995.

While the volume of car production would not increase, Ferrari was looking to increase turnover from royalties generated from merchandising of related goods like T-shirts, caps, Ferrari toy replicas and flags, which it started less than two years ago.
It aims to double its present revenue from merchandising royalties to Singapore $20 million (US$14.3 million) in 1998.
Revenue is also boosted by spare parts sales and from racing events.
Montezemolo said Formula One racing, which Ferrari has maintained as a tradition for the last 50 years, remained important as the company does not advertise.
"The competition Formula One represents for us is the most advanced test of new technical solutions for our GT road cars," said Montezemolo.
